readme.$exec: # Writing the woof README Use this when you write or revise README.md in this repo. The README has two readers. People skim the top and decide in seconds whether to stay. Agents read the whole file through `woof readme` and act on the bottom. Write the top for people, the bottom for agents, and get more technical as the page goes down. ## Process - Work one section at a time: propose an outline, draft the section in the conversation, and write it to the file only after the owner approves. - Keep replies short. Ask one or two questions at most, and recommend instead of listing options. - Apply feedback literally. Then fix the same problem wherever else it appears, and say so. ## Structure Keep these sections in this order: 1. **Opening, with no heading.** The title, then a one-line tagline that names the central idea. Then: - One first-person paragraph in the owner's voice: the problem, told as a story, not a pitch. - One paragraph that explains the idea through the design-system analogy, addressed to the reader. - "You don't run woof. Your agent does:" followed by a chat demo. - One short paragraph with the twist: the same ask in another project gets that project's answer. Mention the companion skill. 2. **How it works.** Show and tell, one level deeper. Each subsection is a short paragraph and one small visual: an illustrative token tree, a one-liner, or a chat demo. No JSON. Escalate: shared defaults and overrides, composition, scripts, discovery and the skill, sharing. 3. **Getting started.** Agent-first and actionable. Requirements in one line, a bootstrap prompt in a copyable code block, then example asks in two groups: filling woof up with primitives, then putting them to work. Each ask is a bold quoted sentence followed by one sentence about what happens. 4. **Under the hood.** The builder pattern: bite-size pieces, one concept per subsection, the simple form first and the full form after it. Leave heavy fields such as `$schemaVersion` for the reference. Explain a concept before any JSON uses it. Use level-4 headings for variants, such as the two places a project can live. 5. **Reference.** Open with one sentence that warns it gets detailed fast. Show the full config first, then tables and rule lists: config schema, commands, scripts, files and folders, limits and decisions. 6. **Development.** One commented code block and a link to the design docs. ## Tone Follow the conversational flavor at the end of these instructions. For this README: - The opening paragraph is the owner's story. Everything after it speaks to the reader. - Show what people ask their agent, not commands they type. - From the Reference heading down, be terse and exact, with no jokes and no images. ## Examples Keep one cast across the README, so each section builds on the last: - Tokens: `git.commits.seven_rules`, `git.commits.conventional`, the alias `git.commit`, the composite `agents.instructions`, and the scripts `git.branch` and `checks.all`. - Projects: `acme`, a team repo with a committed config, and `globex`, a client repo with a private config. - People: Sam, the coworker who imports `globex`. - Use fictional names for projects and people. ## Demos - Show agent conversations as chat images. Keep each transcript in `.github/assets/readme/.txt`, and render it with `pnpm exec tsx .tools/scripts/render-chat.ts .github/assets/readme/.txt .github/assets/readme/.jpg`. - Transcript format: a speaker label, at least two spaces, then the text. `you` or a name is the person, and `agent` is the agent. Agent commands start with `›`, and their output is indented below them. - The script renders a 1024px JPEG in the daisyUI coffee theme from `woof edit`. Don't set a width in the README. GitHub scales the image. - Embed each image as ``. The alt text is one line with no quotes or line breaks, and it describes the whole conversation, including the commands the agent runs. Agents read the raw file, so the alt text is their demo. - Anything the reader copies, such as a prompt to paste, stays a code block. ## Accuracy - Check every command, flag, key, path, and default against the source before you write it. Describe what woof does today, not what's planned. - Don't advertise internal settings, such as `WOOF_HOME`. - Use precise terms. Write "woof configuration", not a bare "project", when you mean the file. Introduce a term before you use it. - Keep limits and decisions apart. A limit is a gap a user can hit. Behavior that matches how design tokens work, or a choice made on purpose, is a decision. ## Format - One line per paragraph, with no hard wraps. - H2 for main sections, H3 for subsections, H4 for variants and reference subsections. - Numbered lists for sequences, and tables for repeated fields. Put `—` in empty table cells. - JSON examples must be valid JSON. - Run `pnpm exec prettier --check README.md` after each change. {{writing.editorial.conversational}}
readme.$description: How to write this repo's README: structure, tone, demos, and reference

release.$exec:
# Release woof to npm

Use this when the owner asks to release a new version of woof. A release is public and permanent: npm never accepts the same version twice. Get one approval covering publication of the agreed version to npm and pushing `master` and its release tag to GitHub. Reuse approval already given in the conversation; do not ask again for each command.

1. Confirm that the working tree is clean and the branch is `master`. Fetch `origin` and confirm that `master` includes `origin/master`. Integrate remote changes if needed. Local release commits may be ahead of `origin/master`.
2. Agree on the version with the owner. Before 1.0, recommend a minor bump for features and breaking changes, and a patch bump for fixes. Reuse a version already chosen for this release.
3. If the version has not already been bumped for this release, {{~npm.version~}}. Otherwise, keep the prepared version.
4. Run `pnpm validate` and `pnpm test` for the prepared changes. Reuse checks that already passed for the same state. Stop if either fails.
5. Run `pnpm pack:check`. Stop if it fails.
6. Commit any remaining version and pin changes by the woof `git.commit` token, with the subject `Release <version>`. If those changes are already committed and the tree is clean, use the prepared commit. Tag it `v<version>`.
7. Show the prepared version and check results. If the owner has not already approved publication and the push, ask once for both.
8. Run `npm publish --browser=false` in a persistent interactive terminal (TTY). If npm prints an authentication URL, show it as a clickable link and keep the command running while the owner approves in their browser. Wait for that same command to finish; browser authentication is not publication. Do not cancel it or ask the owner to rerun the command in another terminal just because authentication is required. If npm requires a fresh login, run `npm login --browser=false` with the same browser approval flow, then retry publication. The package publishes as public, and the pack step builds the bundle first.
9. A successful publish can remain unavailable while npm scans it, usually for about five minutes and sometimes 15 minutes or longer. Poll `npm view @mnbny/woof@<version> version` until it prints the version. Do not publish again just because the registry has not listed it yet. Then, from a directory outside the repo, run `npx --yes @mnbny/woof@<version> --version`. It must print the new version.
10. Under the same release approval, push the commit and the tag with `git push origin master v<version>`.
release.$description: Publish a new woof version to npm

version.$exec:
Bump woof using the patch, minor, or major level requested in the conversation.

Update these together:

1. `package.json` — package version.
2. `README.md` — both npx command pins.
3. `skills/woof-execution/SKILL.md` — both npx pins and the skill version.
4. `skills/woof-living-docs/SKILL.md` — the npx pin.

All woof pins must match the new package version. Increase the execution skill’s integer version only if it hasn’t already advanced for this release.

Review the conversation for any new npx references. If you find additional places that need pins, propose them to the user.

Run `pnpm validate` and report the new version.
version.$description: Bump the woof package version and all recommended npx pins together
